topics.summary: A misplaced decimal point or a mixed unit can change a quantity by 10 or 100 times; some numbers that look decimal, such as hours, feet and overs, are not.

content.text:
3.8 More on the Decimal System
Decimal and Measurement Disasters
Decimal point and unit conversion mistakes may seem minor sometimes but they can lead to serious problems. Here are some actual incidents in which such errors caused major issues.
In 2013, the finance office of Amsterdam City Council (Netherlands) mistakenly sent out €188 million in housing benefits instead of the intended €1.8 million due to a programming error that processed payments in euro cents instead of euros. (1 euro-cent = 1/100 euro).
In 1983, a decimal error nearly caused a disaster for an Air Canada Boeing 767. The ground staff miscalculated the fuel, loading 22,300 pounds instead of kilograms, about half of what was needed (1 pound ~ 0.453 kg). The plane ran out of fuel mid-air, forcing the pilots to make an emergency landing at an abandoned airfield. Fortunately, everyone survived.
Several incidents have occurred due to incorrect reading of decimal numbers while giving medication. For example, reading 0.05 mg as 0.5 mg can lead to using a medicine 10 times more than the prescribed quantity. It is therefore important to pay attention to units and the location of the decimal point.

content.text:
Worked example: In 2013 a council meant to send 1.8 million euros but sent 188 million euros, because payments were processed in euro cents instead of euros. How many times larger was the amount sent? Also, why is 0.05 mg read as 0.5 mg a serious error?
1. 188 million divided by 1.8 million is about 104, so roughly 100 times larger. That matches the slip between cents and euros, where one euro-cent is 1/100 euro.
2. 0.05 mg is 5 hundredths of a mg. 0.5 mg is 5 tenths of a mg.
3. 5 tenths is 10 times 5 hundredths, so reading 0.05 as 0.5 gives a dose 10 times too big.
4. Always check the unit and the place of the decimal point.
Answer: About 100 times larger; the medicine dose would be 10 times larger

content.text:
Worked example: A ground crew loaded 22300 pounds of fuel when 22300 kilograms was needed, and 1 pound is about 0.453 kg. About how many kilograms was loaded, and how does it compare with what was needed?
1. 22300 × 0.453 is about 10102 kg, found by multiplying the pounds by 0.453.
2. What was needed was 22300 kg.
3. 10102 is a little less than half of 22300, so the plane carried about half of the fuel it needed.
4. The unit slip, pounds for kilograms, is the same kind of error as a decimal slip.
Answer: About 10102 kg, about half of what was needed

concepts.concept_name: Decimal and measurement disasters

content.text:
Deceptive Decimal Notation
Sarayu gets a message: “The bus will reach the station 4.5 hours post noon.” When will the bus reach the station: 4:05 p.m., 4:50 p.m., 4:25 p.m.?
None of these! Here, 0.5 hours means splitting an hour into 10 equal parts and taking 5 parts out of it. Each part will be 6 minutes (60 minutes/10) long. 5 such parts make 30 minutes. So, the bus will reach the station at 4:30.
Here is a short-story of a decimal mishap: A girl measures the width of an opening as 2 ft 5 inches but conveys to the carpenter to make a door 2.5 ft wide. The carpenter makes a door of width 2 ft 6 inches (since 1 ft = 12 inches, 0.5 ft = 6 inches), and it wouldn’t close fully.
If you watch cricket, you might have noticed decimal-looking numbers like ‘Overs left: 5.5’. Does this mean 5 overs and 5 balls or 5 overs and 3 balls? Here, 5.5 overs means 5 5/6 overs (as 1 over = 6 balls), i.e., 5 overs and 5 balls.
Where else can we see such ‘non-decimals’ with a decimal-like notation?

1. Predict first: the bus will arrive 4.5 hours after noon. Is it 4:05, 4:25, 4:30 or 4:50?

4. Look for other places where a point is used between two numbers that are not a decimal, such as a time written as hours and minutes.

content.text:
Worked example: A message says the bus reaches at 4.5 hours post noon. When does it arrive? Then, a door was ordered 2.5 ft wide when the opening was 2 ft 5 inches. How wide did the carpenter make it?
1. 0.5 hours is 5 parts out of 10 equal parts of an hour. Each part is 60 ÷ 10 = 6 minutes.
2. 5 parts make 5 × 6 = 30 minutes, so the bus arrives at 4:30 p.m.
3. A foot is 12 inches, so 0.5 ft is half of 12 inches, that is 6 inches.
4. The carpenter made a door 2 ft 6 inches wide, 1 inch too wide for the opening, so it would not close fully.
Answer: 4:30 p.m.; the door was 2 ft 6 inches, 1 inch too wide

content.text:
Worked example: A scoreboard shows 'Overs left: 5.5'. How many overs and balls is that? Then name other places where a point is used but the number is not a decimal.
1. An over has 6 balls, so one ball is 1/6 of an over.
2. 5.5 overs means 5 5/6 overs, that is 5 overs and 5 balls, not 5 overs and 3 balls.
3. Other examples: a time written as 2.30 for 2 hours 30 minutes, a height of 5.11 for 5 feet 11 inches, a date written as 2.10 for the second of October, or version numbers such as 1.10 of an app.
Answer: 5 5/6 overs, that is 5 overs and 5 balls

content.text:
Check the unit and the place of the decimal point before using a number.
A number with a point is a decimal only if each place is worth ten times the next.
Hours, feet and overs are not counted in tens.

topics.summary: Decimal fractions were used in ancient India, modern decimal notation was written down around 950 CE, and the point became the most popular separator in the Indian place value system.

content.text:
A Pinch of History: Decimal Notation Over Time
Decimal fractions (i.e., fractions with denominators like 1/10, 1/100, 1/1000, and so on) are used in the works of a number of ancient Indian astronomers and mathematicians, including in the important 8th century works of Śhrīdharāchārya on arithmetic and algebra.
Decimal notation, in essentially its modern form, was described in detail in Kitāb al-Fuṣūl fī al-Ḥisāb al Hindī (The Book of Chapters on Indian Arithmetic) by Abūl Ḥassan al-Uqlīdisī, an Arab mathematician, in around 950 CE. He represented the number 0.059375 with a small vertical mark placed after the zero that is the whole number part.
In the 15th century, to separate whole numbers from fractional parts, a number of different notations were used: a vertical mark on the last digit of the whole number part (as shown above), use of different colours and a numerical superscript giving the number of fractional decimal places (0.36 would be written as the digits 36 with a small 2 above them).

content.text:
In the 16th century, John Napier, a Scottish mathematician, and Christopher Clavius, a German mathematician, used the point/period (‘.’) to separate the whole number and the fractional parts, while François Viète, a French mathematician, used the comma (‘,’) instead.
Currently, several countries use the comma to separate the integer part and the fractional part. In these countries, the number 1,000.5 is written with a space after the 1 and a comma before the 5 (space as a thousand separator). But the decimal point has endured as the most popular notation for writing numbers having fractional parts in the Indian place value system.

content.text:
Worked example: In a country that uses the comma, how would a number such as one thousand and five tenths be written, and why is it important to know which notation is in use?
1. In the point notation it is 1,000.5, with a comma between thousands and a point before the tenths.
2. In the comma notation the space takes the thousand separator's place and the comma becomes the decimal mark, so it reads 1 000,5.
3. A reader who does not know which notation is used could take the comma as a thousand separator and misread the number, so check the notation first.
Answer: 1 000,5 in the comma notation, and the notation must be checked

content.text:
SUMMARY
We can split a unit into smaller parts to get more exact/accurate measurements.
We extended the Indian place value system and saw that 1 unit = 10 one-tenths, 1 tenth = 10 one-hundredths, 1 hundredth = 10 one-thousandths, 10 one-hundredths = 1 tenth, 100 one-hundredths = 1 unit.
A decimal point (‘.’) is used in the Indian place value system to separate the whole number part of a number from its fractional part.
We also learnt how to compare decimal numbers, locate them on the number line, and perform addition and subtraction on them.

objectives.objective_text: Students read a length that ends between two whole marks of a ruler as units and tenths of a unit, and explain why the unit was split into smaller parts.
Students write a length of whole units and tenths both as a mixed number and as a count of tenths, and read mixed numbers and tenths aloud.
Students arrange lengths written as mixed numbers and as counts of tenths in increasing order by writing them all as counts of tenths.
Students read lengths between whole marks as units and tenths, write them as counts of tenths, and put them in increasing order.
Students add two or more lengths written as units and tenths, regrouping 10 tenths as 1 unit.
Students subtract one length in units and tenths from another, breaking 1 unit into 10 tenths when there are too few tenths.
Students find the constant change in a sequence of numbers written in units and tenths and extend the sequence by four terms.
Students add and subtract lengths written in units and tenths and extend patterns of tenths.
Students explain that splitting each tenth into 10 equal parts gives 100 equal parts in a unit, each a hundredth, and read a length as units, tenths and hundredths.
Students read a length shown on a scale as units, tenths and hundredths, as units and hundredths, and as a count of hundredths, and say it in words.
Students compare lengths written with tenths and hundredths, pick the longest and shortest of a group by writing every length in hundredths, and mark them on a scale.
Students split a tenth into hundredths, read lengths as units, tenths and hundredths, and compare them.
Students add lengths in units, tenths and hundredths by adding place by place and carrying, by converting to hundredths, and compare the methods with the addition of whole numbers.
Students subtract lengths in units, tenths and hundredths, breaking a unit or a tenth where there are too few, and compare the method with subtracting whole numbers.
Students find sums and differences of lengths written in units, tenths and hundredths, carrying and breaking at each place.
Students compare splitting a unit into 4 equal parts with splitting it into 10, and explain why 10 is used every time in the Indian place value system.
Students extend the ladder of places to one-thousandth by splitting a hundredth into 10 equal parts, and say why the system is called decimal.
Students answer how many of a smaller place make one of a bigger place, using the factor of 10 for each step between the places, and make questions of their own.
Students use the factor of 10 between neighbouring places to say how many of a smaller place make one of a bigger place.
Students show that 705 can mean three different quantities if the places are not marked, and explain how a decimal point separates the whole part from the fractional part.
Students read a decimal digit by digit after the point, and write quantities given in places in decimal form with a place value table.
Students write a count of hundreds, tens, tenths or hundredths as a decimal by splitting it into places or by moving the point.
Students write fractions and quantities as decimals, split decimals into tenths, hundredths and thousandths, and read them aloud.
Students convert between millimetres and centimetres and between centimetres and metres by using one tenth and one hundredth as the exchange rates.
Students convert between grams and kilograms with one thousandth as the exchange rate, and between milligrams and grams.
Students convert between paise and rupees with one hundredth as the exchange rate, and compare old and new prices.
Students convert lengths, weights and money between a bigger and a smaller unit by moving the decimal point.
Students locate a decimal on the number line by splitting the unit into 10 equal parts, name the divisions between 1 and 1.1, and read decimals at marks.
Students locate a decimal such as 4.185 by zooming into one gap per digit, read the decimal at the end of a zoom, and draw zoom lines for 9.876 and 0.407.
Students find the value of one division on a line with given end points and use it to read the decimals at marked points.
Students locate decimals by zooming and read the decimals at marked points on lines with different end points.
Students decide whether zeroes written at the right end of a decimal change its value, using a place value table, and tell which decimals among a group are equal.
Students compare two decimals digit by digit from the biggest place, stop at the first place where the digits differ, and explain why the later digits cannot change the answer.
Students find the decimal nearest to a target by comparing the size of each gap, and use a set of digits to make a decimal as close as possible to a target.
Students compare and order decimals place by place and find the decimal closest to a number.
Students add two decimals in the compact column form with the decimal points in one line, carrying from the right, and connect it to the place value working.
Students test Sonu's claim about the range in which the sum of two decimals lies, and use it to check a sum before computing.
Students add decimals with the points in a line, carrying from the right, and check each sum against an estimate.
Students subtract one decimal from another with the points lined up and with borrowing, in the compact form, and connect it to the place value working.
Students narrow down the whole numbers within which the difference of two decimals must lie, and use the range to check a difference.
Students subtract decimals with the points lined up, zeroes filled in and borrowing, and check each difference against an estimate.
Students find the change between terms of a decimal sequence, add or subtract it to extend the sequence, and invent sequences for others to extend.
Students find the rule of a decimal pattern, including one that alternates between two changes, and extend it.
Students explain how a decimal point or a unit slip caused an Amsterdam payment error, a fuel shortage and a medicine error, and how big each error was.
Students read 4.5 hours, 2.5 feet and 5.5 overs correctly, and give other examples of decimal-like numbers that are not decimals.
Students explain how a misplaced decimal point or a unit slip changes a quantity, and read decimal-like numbers of time, feet and overs correctly.
Students tell where decimal fractions first appear in the work of ancient Indian mathematicians, who described modern decimal notation around 950 CE, and what the 15th century notations looked like.
Students explain how the point and the comma were used in the 16th century, and how some countries today write one thousand and five tenths.
Students place the early uses of decimal fractions and decimal notation in order and say how the point and the comma differ.

chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order: smaller units first, then tenths and hundredths as parts of a unit, then the decimal point as a way of writing them, then comparing and computing. Every decimal rule is reached from the fractions the student already knows.

points.text: The hook video leaves Sonu's two screws unmeasured. The tenth, the hundredth and the decimal point arrive only after the student has met a gap that a whole mark cannot name.
points.title: Try first, name later

points.text: A decimal is a count of tenths, hundredths or thousandths. Adding, subtracting and comparing decimals use the same place value moves as whole numbers, so nothing is a trick to remember.
points.title: Fractions underneath every decimal

points.text: On the number line each digit names one more zoom into ten equal parts, and the end marks of a line decide what one division is worth.
points.title: One zoom per digit
